html:
The Enawenê-nawê are an Arawakan people of the Juruena river basin in Mato Grosso, Brazil. They had no lasting contact with outsiders until Jesuit missionaries reached them in 1974.

They fish with large wooden weirs and grow manioc and maize, and they do not eat red meat. Their long Yaokwa ritual, tied to the fish harvest, is on UNESCO's list of heritage in need of urgent protection. They are related by language to the Paresi, and their neighbours include the Nambikwara and the Rikbaktsa. Dams planned on the Juruena have worried them because they would cut off the fish runs.
